paper.title: Structure-aware graph neural network based deep transfer learning framework for enhanced predictive analytics on diverse materials datasets
paper.research_summary: This paper presents a structure-aware graph neural network (GNN) based deep transfer learning framework to improve predictive performance for materials properties using sparse data. It leverages the ALIGNN architecture trained on large source datasets (e.g., Materials Project formation energy) and applies transfer learning—via fine-tuning or feature extraction—to small target datasets across diverse materials classes (3D/2D, inorganic/organic, computational/experimental). The framework is evaluated on 115 dataset-property combinations, showing TL models outperform scratch-trained models in ≈90% of cases, especially for extrapolation and small-data regimes.

tasks.objective: To accurately predict materials properties using crystal structure information, especially when training data is sparse.
constraints: cross-materials class transfer (e.g., crystalline to molecular)
output_goal: numerical prediction of target property value (e.g., eV, GPa, Å, μB)

evidence.text: Accurate materials property prediction using crystal structure occupies a primary and often critical role in materials science, particularly when screening through a near-infinite space of candidate materials for desirable materials performance.

Here we present a framework for materials property prediction tasks using structure information that leverages graph neural network-based architecture along with deep-transfer-learning techniques to drastically improve the model’s predictive ability on diverse materials (3D/2D, inorganic/organic, computational/experimental) data.

stages.stage_goal: Collect large source and small target datasets spanning multiple materials classes and properties.

evidence.text: We use nine datasets of DFT-computed and experimental properties in this work: Materials Project (MP)4, Joint Automated Repository for Various Integrated Simulations (JARVIS) 3D with 46 properties and 2D with 32 properties5, Flla44 with three properties, Dielectric Constant (DC)45 with five properties, Piezoelectric Tensor (PT)46 with two properties, Experimental Formation Energy (EFE)47 with one property, Kingsbury Experimental Formation Energy (KEFE)48 with one property, Kingsbury Experimental Bandgap (KEB)49 with one property, and Harvard Organic Photovoltaic Dataset (HOPV)50 with 24 properties.

stages.stage_name_raw: preprocessing of structure files for GNN input
stages.stage_goal: Convert raw crystal structure files into graph representations suitable for ALIGNN.
stage_input: structure file containing information on lattice geometry and the ionic positions of a compound

evidence.text: The structure ﬁle containing information on lattice geometry and the ionic positions of a compound is divided into atom, bond, and angle-based features before feeding into the ALIGNN-based Feature Extractor where we perform feature extraction.

stages.stage_name_raw: training of source model (ALIGNN) on large dataset
stages.stage_goal: Train a structure-aware GNN (ALIGNN) on formation energy of Materials Project to learn transferable structural representations.

evidence.text: A model trained on the formation energy of the MP dataset39 is used as the source model to perform ﬁne-tuning and feature extraction-based transfer learning as formation energy has shown to lead to meaningful representations from large source datasets36, which can then be applied during the model training on the smaller target datasets to improve their predictive performance.

stages.stage_name_raw: generation of transfer learning models (fine-tuning and feature extraction)
stages.stage_goal: Produce two types of target models: fine-tuned ALIGNN and feature-extracted models using ALIGNN-derived representations.

evidence.text: The transfer of information can be performed by either ﬁne-tuning or feature extraction methods. Fine-tuning uses the weights from the pre-trained model as the preliminary weight initialization for the network, which are further reﬁned using the target dataset. In the feature extraction method, we treat the pre-trained model as a feature extractor to extract robust features for the target dataset and use them to build the target model using representation learning.
Hence, for the rest of the analysis, we only atom-bond-angle features(last) as the feature set to perform feature extraction-based TL for generalizability.

stages.stage_name_raw: evaluation of TL and scratch models on holdout test sets
stages.stage_goal: Quantitatively compare predictive accuracy of TL models against scratch-trained ALIGNN and baseline models using MAE.

evidence.text: The target datasets are randomly split with a ﬁxed random seed into training, validation, and holdout test sets in the ratio of 80:10:10. [...] We use mean absolute error (MAE) as the primary evaluation metric for all models.
We compare models obtained using the proposed framework with models trained from scratch (SC).

stages.stage_name_raw: analysis of feature type impact and dataset-size dependency
stages.stage_goal: Assess relative contribution of atom/bond/angle features and quantify performance gain as function of target dataset size.
stage_input: Supplementary Figures 2 and 3 (dataset size vs. % error improvement)

evidence.text: Table 1 shows that, in general, feature representations containing structure-aware atom-based features tend to perform better as compared to only bond or angle-based features. Moreover, the combination containing the last set of the atom, bond, and angle-based features, called atom-bond-angle features(last), performs the best among the 38 sets of features used for the analysis.

We plot the percent error improvement of the TL model against the SC model as a function of dataset size with a histogram in Supplementary Figures 2 and 3 and observe larger improvement in the model accuracy for smaller datasets as compared to larger datasets.

We use nine datasets of DFT-computed and experimental properties in this work: Materials Project (MP)4, Joint Automated Repository for Various Integrated Simulations (JARVIS) 3D with 46 properties and 2D with 32 properties5, Flla44 with three properties, Dielectric Constant (DC)45 with five properties, Piezoelectric Tensor (PT)46 with two properties, Experimental Formation Energy (EFE)47 with one property, Kingsbury Experimental Formation Energy (KEFE)48 with one property, Kingsbury Experimental Bandgap (KEB)49 with one property, and Harvard Organic Photovoltaic Dataset (HOPV)50 with 24 properties.

JARVIS-2D database
In the previous sections, we used different DFT-computed datasets containing 3D materials to perform the model training using the proposed framework to improve the performance of the target model. However, there also exist a class of materials that exhibit plate-like 2D shapes whose physical and chemical properties may differ in nature from that of 3D materials. Hence, here we investigate the effect of using the same source model trained on 3D materials dataset with TL to build target models on datasets containing 2D materials.
